source.title: Automatic Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Grading using Deep Neural Networks: Comparative Analysis of Network Architectures and Optimization Functions

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports classification accuracy for architecture and optimizer configurations, but does not measure training error, a train–test gap, or the versions’ specific generalization claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports classification accuracy for ten architecture/optimizer configurations. It does not identify those values as held-out test accuracy, compare training with test performance, or use random labels. The optimizer and architecture comparisons also change other settings, so they do not isolate the versioned effects.
record.test_reason: The study compares knee OA classification configurations but provides no within-architecture adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison, convolutional versus fully connected comparison, or other version-specific intervention. The reported accuracy split is unspecified. Its discussion and citations of optimizer generalization do not constitute a test.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors identify EfficientNet-B7 with Nadam as their best configuration at 70.1% accuracy and conclude that deep networks offer potential for automated knee OA grading. They emphasize selecting suitable architectures, optimizers and hyperparameters.
record.recipe_differences: Compares image-classification architectures and optimizer configurations for knee OA grading; it does not test the claim’s interventions or train–test generalization measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported classification accuracy varies across the tested architecture and optimizer configurations; the experiments also vary learning rate, epochs, and batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: Reported knee OA grading accuracy varies across architecture and optimizer configurations, reaching 70.1% with EfficientNet-B7 and Nadam. The accuracy split is unspecified, and no version-specific comparison is established.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and training configuration affect reported knee OA grading accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Applied Engineering and Natural Sciences
record.problems: No training accuracy or explicit generalization-gap measure is reported. The text does not say whether the tabulated accuracy is from the held-out test set. Architecture, optimizer, learning rate, epochs, and batch size vary across configurations, limiting comparisons.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out performance.
Width increases beyond zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning; effects of broader tuning, decoupled weight decay or switching to SGD.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover held-out performance.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus random examples and resulting test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: Training, validation and testing splits are described, but Table 1 does not identify which split supplies its accuracies. A train–test gap is not required to test every version; here the decisive issue is the absence of comparisons measuring the specified claims. Generic AdamW generalization statements cite prior work rather than report this study's evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out performance.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error.
Fully connected image classifiers and the effect of local connectivity.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison on held-out performance; broader tuning, weight-decay changes, switching optimizers, and language benchmarks.
Large versus small batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to the training recipe.
Dropout interventions and their effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the train–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
